Part One

Screenshot & Observe

App selected: Auteur AI Studios (preview--auteur-alchemy.lovable.app) — a luxury creative AI platform I am currently designing. I chose it because its aesthetic has always felt more instinctive than deliberate, and I wanted to find out why.

Hero — full-bleed atmospheric
Arsenal + gallery
The Roster — cinematic figure
Talent cards + CTA
Login modal — dark surface
Full page — scroll view
1
Amber appears exactly once per screen. The CTA button and section accent markers. It never appears decoratively. That singular use is precisely what gives it authority — using it twice would cut its power in half.
2
The interface recedes behind the imagery. Almost no UI chrome is visible — no floating sidebars, no persistent toolbars. The editorial photography and AI-generated imagery fills the screen. The product disappears so the work shows.
3
Copy is stripped to the minimum viable phrase. "The Roster." "Your Creative Arsenal." These read as editorial titles, not feature names. The voice precedes the function — which implies confidence that the function doesn't need explaining.
02
Part Two

AI Analysis

Using Claude to analyze the design system from the screenshots, then pushing back with the three follow-up questions from the brief.

Color System
Primary background: #0D0B0A — not true black, but a warm near-void with brown undertones that reads as luxury rather than tech. A single accent: #C4973F (amber/gold) in two slots only — CTAs and section markers. Supporting text sits in a muted warm gray #9A9189. The palette is monochromatic plus one accent. No blue. No purple. No gradient anywhere.
Typography System
Two-font system. Cormorant Garamond (serif) for all display and section headings — editorial, refined, slightly old-world. DM Sans light/regular for all body copy, labels, captions. Three sizes: 48–96px display, 24–32px section titles, 11px all-caps UI labels. All caps carry 0.15em letter-spacing — the fashion editorial tell. No font above weight 500 anywhere.
Spacing Logic
Base unit 8px. Section padding is 96px vertical — exactly 12 base units. Hero sections push to 140px+. Card internal padding is 24px. The ratios are strict multiples. The generous white space signals that the product doesn't need to sell on every pixel — only brands that are confident can afford to leave this much room empty.
Button Hierarchy
Exactly two states. Primary: amber fill, near-black text, all caps, 0.12em tracking, 2px radius — never pill-shaped. Secondary: transparent with 35% white border, same type treatment. The 2px radius refuses to announce itself. The all-caps + tracking signals editorial instincts over product conventions. The login modal uses the same amber fill for Sign In — system is consistent.

"The most striking finding: this design system assumes the user is already sophisticated. It doesn't explain itself. No tooltips in the hero, no feature callouts with arrows, no trust badges. It speaks to the creative professional you want to be — not where you currently are. That is a specific and confident bet."

— AI Analysis, Follow-up: What assumptions does this system make about its user?
What's Missing — AI Response to Follow-up
No semantic color system. There are no defined states for success, warning, or error. This works at the marketing site level but will become a problem the moment real app functionality ships — file upload errors, generation failures, API rate limits. A more complete version of this system would define error (deep crimson adjacent to the amber warmth), success (muted teal, not green), and warning (deep ochre, distinct from amber). These should feel as considered as the primary palette — not imported from a generic component library as an afterthought.

Base unit: 8px. All spacing is a multiple. Sections breathe at 96px vertical. Hero sections are cinematic — no upper limit on vertical padding.

Voice
Authoritative
States, never explains. Short declarative phrases. No qualifiers, no hedging, no exclamation marks.
Cinematic
Every word earns its place. Atmosphere over information density. Copy reads like a title card.
Aspirational
Speaks to the creative you want to be — not where you currently are. Assumes sophistication.
Button"Get Started" — not "Sign Up For Free Today"
Empty state"Your canvas is waiting." — not "No projects yet. Create one!"
Error"Something went wrong. We're on it." — not "Error 500: Internal Server Error"
Nav label"The Roster" — not "Browse Creatives"
Buttons

Secondary: ghost · 35% white border · identical type treatment

04
Journal Prompt

What did reverse-engineering someone else's system teach you about your own taste?

The honest answer is that I chose my own app because I didn't think it would teach me anything new — I already knew what I'd built. I was wrong.

Reverse-engineering it forced me to name things I had only felt. I knew I wanted the site to feel like a fashion magazine and not like a startup. But I didn't have language for why I kept deleting elements. Going through the system analytically, I can finally say it: my instinct is subtraction. When I'm unsatisfied with something I've built, I'm almost never adding — I'm looking for what to remove. The amber button worked the moment it was the only amber thing on the page. The serif headline worked the moment I stopped bolding it.

What surprised me was the consistency of the restraint. I had made dozens of micro-decisions — 2px border radius on buttons, no pill shapes, 300 font weight as the default, Cormorant Garamond over a more common display serif — and they all pointed to the same underlying value: don't announce yourself. A design that tries to impress you every second impresses you not at all.

The AI analysis surfaced something uncomfortable: the system has no language for failure. No error states, no semantic feedback colors. That's a tell. When you're building aspirationally — for what the product could be, not what it currently is — you don't spend time designing error messages. You're building the fantasy version. A more complete system would require sitting with the unglamorous states. That's the work that's actually harder than the hero section.
